# Session 5: Advanced Database Search & Profile Methods

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Profile drift

> PSI-BLAST is like social media: after a few iterations, everything it finds agrees with it.
:::

## Learning goals

By the end of this session you should be able to explain why exact
dynamic programming doesn't scale to searching a whole database and
describe BLAST's seed-extend-evaluate heuristic and how MMseqs2 scales
the same ideas; interpret a real BLAST
result's E-value and bit score; construct a small position-specific
scoring matrix (PSSM) by hand, including why pseudocounts matter;
describe PSI-BLAST as BLAST iterated with a PSSM instead of a single
sequence, including why iteration can drift; and explain, at a conceptual level, what a profile Hidden
Markov Model adds beyond a PSSM.

## The scaling problem, and BLAST's heuristic answer

Session 4's dynamic programming finds the *provably optimal* alignment
between two sequences, but it costs time proportional to the product of
their lengths. That's fine for two sequences a few hundred residues long.
It is not fine for searching one query against a database — GenBank and
UniProt hold well over a hundred million sequences between them — where
running full dynamic programming against every single entry would take
far too long to be useful.

**BLAST** (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool) trades the guarantee of
optimality for speed: instead of exhaustively filling a DP matrix for
every database sequence, it looks for short, exact-or-near-exact matches
first, and only spends the expensive alignment step on the promising
regions those matches point to. Concretely, BLAST runs in three stages:

1. **Seeding** — break the query into short "words", list every word
   that scores well against each of them, and scan the database for
   occurrences of those words.
2. **Extension** — grow each seed hit outward, in both directions, into
   a full local alignment.
3. **Evaluation** — ask whether the resulting alignment's score is
   better than what pure chance would produce.

Each stage is covered in its own section below. This three-stage picture
is the core idea, deliberately simplified: production BLAST adds
refinements such as the *two-hit* rule (only extend when two seeds lie
close together on the same diagonal), masking of low-complexity regions,
gapped extension, and corrections for unusual amino-acid composition.
None of them changes the logic of seed, extend, evaluate.

### Further reading

- Wikipedia, [BLAST (biotechnology)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BLAST_(biotechnology))
- NCBI, [BLAST Help](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK1762/) — the practical reference for choosing blastp/blastn/blastx and reading real output

## Stage 1: seeding — turning the query into fast lookups

For protein sequences, a "word" is usually just 3 residues long. A query
of length 200 therefore has 198 overlapping 3-letter words. For each one,
BLAST doesn't search the database for an *exact* match only — using a
substitution matrix (BLOSUM62, from Session 4), it precomputes every 3-letter
combination that scores *above a threshold* $T$ against the query word,
since a biologically real match may substitute a residue or two without
losing significance.

**Worked example.** For the query word `LWG` scored against the real
BLOSUM62 matrix, several other words also clear a typical threshold of
$T=12$ (computed directly from BLOSUM62 in the notebook — 49 words clear
this threshold in total; the top ones):

| Neighbor word | Score vs. `LWG` |
|---|---|
| `LWG` | 21 |
| `IWG` | 19 |
| `MWG` | 19 |
| `VWG` | 18 |
| `FWG` | 17 |
| `AWG` | 16 |
| `CWG` | 16 |
| `TWG` | 16 |
| `YWG` | 16 |
| `KWG` | 15 |

These query words and their high-scoring neighbours go into a **lookup
table**, built once per query: for every 3-letter word, the table records
which query positions it would seed. BLAST then scans each database
sequence once, from start to end, and for every 3-letter word it reads
asks the table "does this word seed anything in the query, and where?"
That check is a single table lookup, so the scan is fast and linear in
the size of the database, and only the few places that produce a seed go
on to the expensive extension step.

## Stage 2: extension — growing a seed into a real alignment

A seed hit is just a 3-letter coincidence — not yet evidence of anything.
BLAST extends it outward in both directions, recomputing a running score
as it goes, using the same substitution-matrix logic as Session 4's dynamic
programming but without filling a full matrix: it stops as soon as the
running score has fallen too far below its own best point so far.

**The X-drop rule.** Track the *running score* as the alignment extends,
and separately track the *best score seen so far*. If the running score
ever falls more than a threshold $X$ below that running best, stop
extending — the alignment is very unlikely to recover — and trim the
reported alignment back to wherever the running best actually occurred.

**Worked example**, adapted from Korf, Yandell & Bedell (2003): treat two
short strings as if they were sequences, scoring $+1$ for a matching
character and $-1$ for a mismatch (spaces ignored), with $X=5$:

```
query:    Thequickbrownfoxjumps...
database: Thequietbrownncatpurrs...
```

The running score climbs steadily through `Thequ`, dips slightly at the
`ick`/`iet` mismatch, recovers and climbs further through `brown` to a
peak of **9** right after `...brown`/`...brown`, then falls steadily as
`foxjump` diverges from `catpurr`. By the time the running score has
dropped 5 points below that peak of 9, extension stops — and the
reported alignment is trimmed back to the peak itself: `Thequickbrown`
paired with `Thequietbrown`, not the lower-scoring tail beyond it. The
notebook reproduces this computation in code.

## Stage 3: is this hit significant? E-values and bit scores

Extending every seed produces a raw alignment score — but a raw score
alone doesn't say whether the alignment is *meaningful* or just what you'd
expect from two random sequences of that length. Scores from aligning a
query against random sequence data follow an **extreme value (Gumbel)
distribution** — not a normal distribution — a result Karlin and Altschul
proved in 1990 and that underpins BLAST's statistics.

From that distribution, the expected number of alignments scoring at
least $S$ purely by chance — the **E-value** — is

$$
E = K m n\, e^{-\lambda S}
$$

where $m$ and $n$ are the lengths of the query and the database, and $K$ and $\lambda$ are constants of the particular scoring
system (substitution matrix and gap penalties) — reported directly in
real BLAST output as "Karlin-Altschul statistics." This is the simplified
textbook form: real BLAST replaces $m$ and $n$ by slightly smaller
*effective* lengths (an alignment cannot start right at the end of a
sequence) and adjusts for composition, but the behaviour is the same.
Two consequences matter: a higher score gives an exponentially smaller
$E$, and a bigger database ($n$) inflates $E$
for the *same* alignment, since chance has more opportunities to produce
a false hit — this is why an E-value is only meaningful together with the
database it was computed against, and why the same alignment can be
"significant" against a small database but not against all of GenBank.

Raw scores and E-values both depend on which scoring system was used,
which makes them awkward to compare across different searches. The
**bit score** fixes this by normalizing away the scoring system:

$$
S' = \frac{\lambda S - \ln K}{\ln 2}
$$

Bit scores from completely different searches — even ones using different
substitution matrices — can be compared directly. A bit score is not a
significance test on its own, though: there is no universal bit-score
cutoff, because whether a given score is surprising still depends on how
large a search space it was found in. For significance, read the E-value.

**Reading real output.** Running a real local BLASTP search of *HBB*
(beta-globin, `P68871`) against its five closest human globin relatives
gives:

| Hit | % identity | E-value | Bit score |
|---|---|---|---|
| Delta-globin (`HBD`) | 93.2% | 9.3×10⁻¹⁰⁵ | 284 |
| Epsilon-globin (`HBE`) | 75.5% | 2.1×10⁻⁸⁷ | 240 |
| Alpha-globin (`HBA`) | 43.4% | 9.0×10⁻³⁸ | 114 |
| Zeta-globin (`HBAZ`) | 35.9% | 3.8×10⁻³² | 100 |
| Myoglobin (`MYG`) | 16.0% | 63 | 10.8 |

The first four are all confident, high-quality hits — high percent
identity, astronomically small E-values, comfortably high bit scores.
Myoglobin is the interesting case. It shares the globin fold and a real
evolutionary origin with hemoglobin, yet BLAST reports only a weak
alignment with an E-value of 63: taken at face value, no statistical
evidence at all. But that number only evaluates the alignment BLAST
*found*. Run the same search with the two-hit rule switched off (every
single seed gets extended; `-window_size 0` in BLAST+) and BLAST finds a
full-length alignment, 145 residues at 25.5% identity, with an E-value of
5×10⁻¹¹. With the default settings no pair of seeds happened to fall
close enough together on the right diagonal, so the good alignment was
never extended. This is the price of a heuristic: BLAST is fast because
it skips most of the search, and occasionally it skips the answer. An
optimal Smith–Waterman search would not have missed it.

Database size still matters too. These E-values are relative to a tiny
five-sequence database; against a database the size of UniProtKB (about
$9\times10^{10}$ residues) the same full-length myoglobin alignment
would get an E-value of about 0.007 — significant, but only just.
Relatives that have diverged further than myoglobin, such as the
bacterial *truncated* hemoglobins, give no detectable pairwise signal at
all, even with the optimal alignment (Session 6 shows that they still
share the globin fold).

### Further reading

- Wikipedia, [E-values](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-value)
- Original source: Karlin & Altschul (1990), *PNAS* 87:2264-2268 — the full derivation behind the formula above

## BLAST's ideas at modern database scale: MMseqs2

BLAST was designed in 1990, when the protein databases held tens of
thousands of sequences. Today's metagenomic collections hold billions,
and even BLAST becomes too slow. **MMseqs2** (Steinegger & Söding, 2017)
is a widely used modern search tool that keeps BLAST's logic but turns
one part of it around. In simplified form:

1. **Index the target database by short words** (k-mers, typically 6–7
   residues for proteins): a table that maps each k-mer to the database
   sequences and positions where it occurs, built once and reused.
2. For each k-mer in the query, generate the **similar** k-mers (scored
   with a substitution matrix, exactly like BLAST's neighbour words) and
   look them up in the index.
3. Keep only database sequences where **two matching k-mers fall on the
   same diagonal** — the same offset between query and target position,
   just as in a dot plot from Session 4. Two consistent hits are much
   stronger evidence of a real alignment than one.
4. Score the surviving candidates quickly with an **ungapped alignment**
   along that diagonal, and discard the weak ones.
5. Run the expensive **gapped Smith–Waterman** alignment, heavily
   optimized to use the processor's vector instructions, only on the
   small set that is left.

The difference from classic BLAST is which side gets indexed. BLAST
builds a lookup table from the *query* and its neighbour words, and then
reads through every database sequence. MMseqs2 indexes the *database*
once, so each query only has to look up its own k-mers. Steps 3–5 are a
cascade of ever more expensive filters, each passing on only a small
fraction of the candidates. The result is often hundreds of times faster
than BLAST at similar sensitivity. There is no machine learning
involved, just the same seed-extend-evaluate ideas engineered for scale.
Like PSI-BLAST below, MMseqs2 can also iterate, turning its hits into a
profile and searching again; ColabFold uses it to build the alignments
AlphaFold needs (Session 12). Session 6 meets its structural counterpart,
Foldseek, from the same group.

## From one sequence to many: PSI-BLAST and the PSSM

Myoglobin sits near the edge of what a single sequence can detect, and
more distant relatives lie beyond it. Ordinary BLAST scores everything
against one fixed substitution matrix, no matter which family the query
belongs to, so a faint but real family signal is easily lost against
the background of a large database. **PSI-BLAST**
(Position-Specific Iterated BLAST) does better by building a
*query-specific* scoring matrix and refining it over several rounds:

1. Run an ordinary BLAST search with the query sequence.
2. Take the hits that pass the **inclusion threshold** (an E-value
   cutoff, by default stricter than the one used for *reporting* hits),
   align them to the query, and turn that alignment into a
   **position-specific scoring matrix (PSSM)** — described below. Hits
   that are displayed but fall short of the inclusion threshold do not
   enter the profile.
3. Search the database again, this time scoring with the PSSM instead of
   a generic substitution matrix.
4. Repeat: each round's included hits refine the PSSM further, until no
   new sequences pass the threshold (convergence) or a set number of
   rounds is reached.

This is more sensitive than a single BLAST pass, particularly for finding
*remote* homologs whose similarity to the original query is too faint for
a fixed substitution matrix to catch.

**Iteration is not automatically better: profile drift.** If one
unrelated sequence passes the inclusion threshold, it enters the
alignment and shifts the next PSSM a little towards itself. The next
round then finds more sequences like the intruder, which shift the
profile further, and after a few rounds the "family" can be dominated by
proteins that have nothing to do with the original query — often through
a shared low-complexity or coiled-coil region rather than real homology.
This is a general lesson that returns in the machine-learning half of
the course: a model is only as good as the examples it was built from,
and a model that chooses its own training data can reinforce its own
mistakes. In practice: keep the inclusion threshold strict, look at what
entered each round, and check surprising late-round hits independently.

### Building a PSSM, step by step

Session 4 ended with alignment columns, their entropy, and sequence
logos. A logo *describes* an alignment column; a PSSM turns those same
column statistics into numbers that can *score* a new sequence. The
recipe below is a teaching model — the real PSI-BLAST computation also
weights sequences and uses more sophisticated pseudocounts, as noted
along the way — but every step has the same purpose in the real thing.

**1. Count.** From a multiple sequence alignment, count how often each
residue appears at each position. Take this small 5-sequence toy
alignment:

```
Position:   1 2 3 4 5
Protein 1:  A G L S P
Protein 2:  A G L T P
Protein 3:  R G I S P
Protein 4:  A A L S Q
Protein 5:  A A L S P
```

At position 1: 4 of 5 sequences have `A`, 1 has `R`. At position 5: 4
have `P`, 1 has `Q`. And so on.

Real alignments are rarely this balanced. If a search returns fifty
nearly identical mammalian sequences and three distant ones, raw counts
would make the profile describe mammals, not the family. Real tools
therefore **reduce redundancy or weight sequences**: near-duplicates are
removed or down-weighted so that an over-represented subfamily does not
dominate the counts. The exact recipe varies between programs; the
principle is what matters.

**2. Add pseudocounts.** Turning raw counts straight into frequencies
causes two problems: a residue that never appears at a position gets a
frequency of exactly zero, and its log-odds score becomes $-\infty$; and
with only 5 sequences, a residue's absence might just be bad luck rather
than a real biological signal. **Pseudocounts** — adding a small constant
to every count, before computing frequencies — fix both. In our teaching
model we add $+1$ uniformly to every residue type's count at every
position. Conceptually, a pseudocount is a **prior**: what we assume
about a column before looking at the alignment (here "every residue is
possible"). With only five sequences the prior has a large influence;
with hundreds of sequences the observed counts swamp it. Real tools use
smarter priors, for example giving residues that substitute easily for
the observed ones (according to a substitution matrix) larger
pseudocounts.

**3. Compare to background.** Compute each residue's **background
frequency** $q_j$ — how often it occurs in proteins generally (e.g.
alanine ≈7.4%, tryptophan ≈1.3%) — independent of this alignment.

**4. Compute log-odds scores.** For each position $i$ and residue $j$,

$$
S_{i,j} = \log_2 \frac{f_{i,j}}{q_j}
$$

where $f_{i,j}$ is the (pseudocount-adjusted) observed frequency. Base 2
means a score of $+1$ means "twice as likely here as by chance," $+3$
means "8× as likely," and so on. Arrange $S_{i,j}$ into a matrix — one
row per alignment position, one column per residue (some tools store it
the other way round; the orientation is only a storage convention) — and
that matrix *is* the PSSM: scoring a candidate sequence against it means
looking up one value per position and **summing**, the
weighted-sum/dot-product idea from Session 1, generalized to sequence
positions.

The notebook builds this PSSM from the alignment above and confirms
that the highest-scoring sequence the matrix can produce is `AGLSP` — the
alignment's own consensus, as it should be.

**Why pseudocounts really matter.** Without them, a residue that appears
just *once* at a position, but happens to be biologically rare overall,
can score *higher* than a well-conserved, common residue at another
position — purely because rarity in the background makes any observation
of it look surprising. Concretely: at a position where 4 of 5 sequences
show alanine (background frequency 7.4%) and 1 shows the much rarer
tryptophan (background frequency 1.3%), alanine's raw log-odds score is
$\log_2(0.8/0.074) \approx 3.43$, but tryptophan's is
$\log_2(0.2/0.013) \approx 3.94$ — the single rare occurrence outscores
the four common ones. Pseudocounts damp this effect.

**Gaps.** A PSSM itself only contains substitution scores, one row per
position. To align a new sequence to it, PSI-BLAST uses ordinary gapped
alignment — the same dynamic programming as Session 4, with the PSSM row
for position $i$ taking the place of the substitution-matrix row for
query residue $i$ — and ordinary gap-open and gap-extension penalties,
the same at every position.

**A PSSM is already a linear model.** For an ungapped sequence
$x = x_1 x_2 \dots x_L$, the PSSM score is

$$
S(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{L} w[i, x_i],
$$

where $w[i, x_i]$ is the matrix entry for residue $x_i$ at position $i$:
look up one weight per position and add them. Session 7 keeps this
weighted-sum idea but *learns* the weights from labelled examples
instead of deriving them from alignment counts.

## Profile Hidden Markov Models: what a PSSM still can't represent

A PSSM gives position-specific *substitution* scores, while gaps are
handled separately by the alignment algorithm, with the same penalties
everywhere. Real families are not like that: a loop between two helices
may tolerate insertions of any length, while the core of the domain
almost never has one. A **profile Hidden Markov Model (profile HMM)**
integrates position-specific match, insertion and deletion behaviour
into one probabilistic model of the family, using three kinds of states
arranged in a repeating unit, one per alignment position:

- **Match (M)** states — a conserved position, with its own
  per-residue emission probabilities, playing the same role as one column
  of a PSSM.
- **Insert (I)** states — extra residues between conserved positions,
  which the model can emit and then loop on to allow more than one.
- **Delete (D)** states — a skipped conserved position, emitting
  nothing at all.

Special **Begin** and **End** states bookend the model, and transitions
connect consecutive positions' M/I/D states together (e.g. $M_i \to
M_{i+1}$, $M_i \to I_i$, $M_i \to D_{i+1}$), each with its own learned
probability.

**Why "hidden."** Given an observed residue in a real sequence, the model
never directly tells you whether it came from a Match state or an Insert
state — that has to be *inferred* from which path through the states best
explains the whole sequence, using the emission and transition
probabilities together. The states generate what you observe; they
themselves stay hidden.

This is the extra structure PSSMs lack, and it's why profile HMMs
(not PSSMs) are the standard tool behind large-scale protein family
databases like **Pfam**: a profile HMM trained on a protein family can
recognize a new sequence as a member even when it has a genuinely
different number of residues at a variable region, because the model
itself has learned *where* insertions and deletions are common in that
family, something a PSSM with uniform gap penalties can only
approximate.

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## What neither a PSSM nor a profile HMM can represent

Both score a sequence position by position: the score is a sum over
columns, so each position contributes independently of the others. Real
proteins do not always work that way. When mutations interact, so that
the effect of one depends on the residue at another position
(**epistasis**), no profile can capture it. Session 9 shows a protein
where this matters (all 160,000 variants at four positions of GB1), and
Session 12 shows how pairwise models fitted to an alignment (direct
coupling analysis) add those interactions.
:::

## Worked example: a real profile-HMM hit on *HBB*

Tying this back to the *HBB* (beta-globin) locus from Session 3: searching
Pfam's library of profile HMMs against the real UniProt entry `P68871`
(HBB_HUMAN) — fetched live via EBI's InterPro API — finds a match to
**PF00042 ("Globin")**, spanning residues 27-142 of the 147-residue
protein, with an E-value around $1.3\times10^{-29}$ (in a database of
this size, essentially no match that good is expected by chance). That's a profile HMM doing, on a real sequence and at
production scale, what the toy PSSM above did on paper: scoring
how well a sequence matches a family, position by position.

## The lab

**Full lab**, covering BLAST and profile methods as one continuous
exercise (Session 4 now has its own short lab for alignment practice, so
this one no longer needs to cover that too): identify a real, unknown
gene from a raw sequence via a real NCBI BLAST search (it turns out to
be a sixth real human globin-family gene, continuing this course's own
running thread), then three real code exercises — a real ClustalW
alignment and PSSM on five globin-family proteins, a real PSI-BLAST
search comparing its first iteration against its third against a real
local copy of the PDB, and a live Pfam domain search for HIV-1's
Gag-Pol polyprotein via the same real InterPro API this page's own HBB
worked example uses.

**Recommended: run this for real on the shared course server**, not
just in Colab — the bioinformatics tools these exercises use
(`clustalw`, `psiblast`) are real command-line programs. On Colab the
notebook installs them first; on the course server they are already
installed. Running them over a real
SSH connection (see Session 2's "Connecting to the shared course server")
is a real, transferable skill in its own right. Once connected via
VSCode, either open
[`notebooks/session05-lab.ipynb`](https://colab.research.google.com/github/ElofssonLab/kb8029-book/blob/main/notebooks/session05-lab.ipynb)
there directly (VSCode's Jupyter support runs it on the server, not
your laptop), or open a terminal alongside it and run the same commands
by hand. Colab still works if you don't have server access set up yet
— same notebook either way.

## What's next

A remote homolog can become impossible to recognize from sequence while
its fold stays conserved. Session 6 turns to structure: the four levels
of protein structure, explored hands-on in PyMOL, structure alignment,
and structural search with Foldseek. Session 7 then returns to the
weighted sum $S(x) = \sum_i w[i, x_i]$ that a PSSM computes, formalizes it
as a **perceptron**, and shows that its weights can be *learned* from labelled
examples by gradient descent instead of derived from alignment
statistics the way this session's PSSM was.
